title: Decode String
statement: Given an encoded string, return its decoded form. The encoding rule is k[encoded_string], meaning the bracketed text is repeated exactly k times. k is a positive integer, brackets may nest, the input is always well formed, and digits appear only as repeat counts — never inside the decoded text.
realWorld: Run-length and macro expansion in template engines and config formats work exactly this way, and so does any nested-directive preprocessor. The same shape appears when expanding glob braces in a shell ({a,b}{1,2}) or unrolling a nested loop body in a code generator: an inner construct must be finished before the outer one can use it.

examples.explanation: Two independent blocks at the top level, expanded left to right.
Nested. The inner 2[c] must become "cc" before the outer block knows what it is repeating: "a" + "cc" = "acc", then tripled.
Plain text outside any bracket is simply carried along, and the trailing "ef" belongs to no block at all.

constraints: s contains only lowercase letters, digits and the brackets [ ]
1 <= k <= 300 and the decoded string fits comfortably in memory
The input is always a valid encoding

bruteForce.idea: Repeatedly find an innermost block — a '[' with no other '[' before its matching ']' — expand it in place, and restart the scan on the rewritten string. Stop when no brackets remain.
code: open = i;                          // the last '[' before a ']' is the innermost one
break;                             // rebuild the whole string, then rescan from 0
if (!expanded) break;                      // no bracket pair left to expand

complexity.time: O(d * m) where d is the nesting depth and m the length of the decoded output

bruteForce.whySlow: Each expansion rebuilds the whole string with substring concatenation and then the scan starts over at index 0. Every character of the already-decoded prefix is re-read and re-copied once per remaining bracket level, even though nothing about it can ever change again — it is finished text being carried through the machine over and over. On "3[3[3[3[a]]]]" the growing output is copied top to bottom four times, and the scan re-confirms 'these are plain letters' on the same characters on every pass.

patternIdentification: Nesting is the signal. A new '[' means the block you were building has to be suspended — you are not finished with it, but you cannot continue until something else completes — and the matching ']' means resume it with the inner result in hand. Suspending and resuming work in strictly last-opened-first-closed order is a stack of *unfinished contexts*, not a stack of values. Push what you will need in order to resume (here: the text so far, and the repeat count), clear the workspace, and on the close pop the context back and fold the finished piece into it.

optimized.idea: Two stacks and one working buffer. Walk the string once. A digit extends the pending count (count = count * 10 + digit, so 12[a] means twelve). A '[' suspends: push the pending count onto the counts stack and the text-so-far onto the strings stack, then reset both to empty so the inner block builds in a clean workspace. A ']' resumes: pop the outer text and the count, append the just-finished buffer to the outer text that many times, and make that the new buffer. A letter just appends. Trace "3[a2[c]]": '3' sets count=3; '[' pushes (3, "") and clears, buffer=""; 'a' gives buffer="a"; '2' sets count=2; '[' pushes (2, "a") and clears, buffer=""; 'c' gives buffer="c"; the first ']' pops (2, "a") and folds "c" twice into "a", buffer="acc"; the second ']' pops (3, "") and folds "acc" three times, buffer="accaccacc". The buffer at the end is the answer.
code: count = count * 10 + (c - '0');   // counts can be multi-digit: 12[a] is twelve, not one then two
for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) outer.append(current);

complexity.time: O(m) where m is the length of the decoded output

code: counts.pop();   // ']' always closes the innermost open bracket first
for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) outer.append(current);

commonMistakes: Reading a digit as `count = c - '0'` instead of `count = count * 10 + (c - '0')` — "12[a]" decodes to "aa" rather than twelve a's, and because every single-digit test still passes the bug reaches production.

Not resetting `current` to a fresh builder after pushing it on '[' — the outer text leaks into the inner block and gets repeated with it, so "xy2[a]" comes back as "xyxyaxya" instead of "xyaa". The symptom is text before a bracket appearing duplicated.

Handling ']' by repeating the buffer in place and dropping the popped prefix (`current = current.repeat(times)`) — the block before the current one is discarded entirely, so "2[abc]3[cd]ef" returns "cdcdcdef" with the "abcabc" silently missing.
